name: Republic of Venice
summary: A maritime republic, La Serenissima, that became one of Europe’s great commercial and naval powers. For 1,100 years it traded between Europe and the East until Napoleon ended it in 1797.

location.value: Venice in north-east Italy, with lands in Istria, Dalmatia, the Adriatic and Ionian islands, and at times Crete and Cyprus.

terrain.value: A lagoon city on islands, protected by water.

climate.value: Humid subtropical, with foggy winters and occasional floods (acqua alta).

resources.value: Salt, glass sand, timber from the mainland.

disasters.value: The Black Death (1348) and later plagues.

population.value: About 100,000–180,000 in the city at its height.

urbanisation.value: Venice was one of Europe’s largest cities.

disease.value: Plague of 1575–1577 killed about a third of the city.

economicBase.value: Maritime trade, banking, glass and shipbuilding.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with Constantinople, Alexandria and the Levant in spices and silk.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: The gold ducat (from 1284), trusted across Europe.

inequality.value: A closed noble class ruled after the “Closing of the Great Council” (1297).

governmentType.value: An aristocratic republic led by an elected Doge.

succession.value: Doges elected for life by a complex process.

institutions.value: The Doge, the Great Council, the Senate and the secretive Council of Ten.

stability.value: Remarkably stable for about 1,100 years, with no successful revolution.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between noble families, kept in check by complex voting rules.

armyAndTech.value: The Arsenal could build a galley in a day.

majorWars.value: Fourth Crusade (1204), wars with Genoa and the Ottomans; Lepanto (1571).

territoryChange.value: Gained a large part of north-east Italy and the eastern Adriatic.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals included Genoa (four wars) and the Ottoman Empire.

inventions.value: Mass shipbuilding at the Arsenal; early patents (1474).

scienceEducation.value: A leading centre of book printing (Aldus Manutius’s Aldine Press, 1494); the University of Padua.

openness.value: Open to trade with the Islamic world and Asia, while defending its Catholic identity.

religion.value: Catholic Christianity, with a strong independent streak towards the Pope.

languageWriting.value: Venetian and Italian; Latin for law and learning.

artsArchitecture.value: St Mark’s Basilica, Doge’s Palace; Titian, Tintoretto.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to “the Most Serene Republic” and its patron saint, Mark.

neighbours.value: Byzantium, the Ottomans, the Holy Roman Empire.

colonisation.value: Overseas colonies (the Stato da Mar) such as Crete, Cyprus and Dalmatian ports.

riseSignals.value: By tradition its first doge was elected in 697; it grew as a trading port between Byzantium and the West.

peakPeriod.value: The 13th–16th centuries, when it dominated trade in the eastern Mediterranean.

declineSignals.value: Wars with the Ottomans and the shift of trade to the Atlantic.

outcome.value: Ended by Napoleon in 1797 and handed to Austria.

sources.value: State archives. Checked against Wikipedia (“Republic of Venice”).
